## Today's Agenda

- What tonight is for, and why it is the least enjoyable evening of the semester
- Why only 36 percent of studies could be redone
- Reproducibility defined, and why code beats clicking
- The four tools, one at a time, and the order to install them

## What Tonight Is For

- By the time you leave this room you will have four programs installed and talking to each other, and one file that proves it
- That is the whole goal. Everything else on these slides explains why we bother

## The Least Enjoyable Evening of the Semester

- Installing software is not research. It is the tedious part that makes research possible
- **Something will break for somebody in this room.** It happens every section, every term
- When it breaks it is not a verdict on you. It is one version number disagreeing with another
- We fix it together, tonight, in the room. That is why we do it here and not at home

## The Reason, in One Sentence

Six weeks from now you will look at a number in your own draft and not remember where it
came from.

Everything tonight exists to make that impossible.

## What That Looks Like at Scale

[Open Science Collaboration, 2015]{.eyebrow}

- 270 researchers set out to redo **100 published psychology studies**
- They used the same published methods, similar participants, and the same analyses
- Only **36 percent** replicated at conventional thresholds
- Among those that did, effect sizes averaged about **half** the original
- These were not careless people. Their work simply was not built to be retraced

## What Blocked Them Was Friction, Not Fraud

- Methods sections did not say enough to re-run the analysis
- Researchers had to email the original authors to ask
- Some authors had moved, and some had lost the data
- Some had used software whose menus had since changed

## Reproducibility, Defined

- **Reproducibility** means the analysis can be re-run, by you or by anyone else, and it produces the same result
- It is not a virtue. It is a property of how you stored your work
- The test is small and personal: can you recover, six months from now, exactly what produced a number?

## Why Clicking Loses

- SPSS, Excel, and JMP work through menus and dialog boxes
- You click Analyze, then Compare Means, then One-Way ANOVA, and the result appears
- **The click history vanishes**
- Redoing it next month means remembering which menus, in what order, with which options
- Writing it down means describing every click in prose, and nobody does this well

The course's VS Code menus are different: each one writes its R code into your script, so the record stays.

## Why Code Wins

- A script is a description of every step, in a language a computer can re-run
- **The code is the methods section.** That is the entire argument for everything we install tonight
- Reinhart and Rogoff, the spreadsheet error from last week, was caught only because the file was eventually shared
- Written as code, it would have been visible from the first day

## Tool 1 of 4: VS Code

- **What it is:** a text editor, free, from Microsoft
- **What it does for you:** it is the one window where everything lives
    - Your writing, your code, your files, and your output, so you stop alt-tabbing between five programs
- You will spend more time in this than in anything else this term. It is the desk, not the work

## Tool 2 of 4: R

- **What it is:** a programming language built for data and statistics
- **What it does for you:** it counts things, tests things, and draws charts, and it leaves a written record of having done so
- You are not becoming a programmer. You are learning to drive one tool for one job, the way you learned to drive a citation manager

## Tool 3 of 4: Quarto

- **What it is:** a publishing system
- **What it does for you:** you write one file holding both your prose and your code, press render, and it produces a finished document with the charts already in place
- You never again paste a chart into Word, find an error, redo the chart, and paste it again

## Tool 4 of 4: Git and GitHub

- **What it is:** Git records every change you make, and GitHub keeps that record online
- **What it does for you:** an undo button that reaches back months, and proof of when you did what
- It is also the closest thing our field has to a portfolio. Employers look, so use a professional username

## Install in This Order

1. **[R](https://cran.r-project.org/)**, from cran.r-project.org
2. **[VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/)**, from code.visualstudio.com
3. **The R extension** inside VS Code, by REditorSupport
4. **[Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)**, from quarto.org
5. **The Quarto extension** inside VS Code
6. **[Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads)**, from git-scm.com
7. **The AURA Lab R Companion** inside VS Code: Extensions view > search AURA Lab R Companion > Install

## Why This Order

- Click a name on the previous slide to open its download page. Steps 3, 5, and 7 happen inside VS Code, not in a browser
- The order is not decorative. Each one looks for the one before it and gets confused when it is missing

## Make Your GitHub Account

- **GitHub** is a website that stores your files and their history. Git is the program on your laptop, and GitHub is the copy online
- You need the account before Git is any use to you

1. Sign up at [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup). Choose a **professional username**, because employers will read it
2. Add a profile photo and a short profile README saying who you are and what you study
3. Claim the free [Student Developer Pack](https://education.github.com/pack) with your SIUE email

The pack includes **GitHub Copilot**. The course workspace tells Copilot Chat to write tidyverse code with `%>%` and to remind you to log each exchange in your AI-use log.

The Hub walks through it one step at a time: [GitHub Setup](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/github-setup.html)

## Make Your Workspace Folder

One folder holds everything you write this term. You copy ours rather than building it.

1. Open the [v2v-workspace template](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-workspace)
2. Click the green **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**. Name it `mc501-workspace` and leave it **Public**
3. In VS Code press `Ctrl+Shift+P`, or `Cmd+Shift+P` on a Mac, type **Git: Clone**, press Enter, and paste your new repository's URL
4. When VS Code offers the workspace's recommended extensions, click **Install All**. That includes the AURA Lab R Companion

**You should see:** your folder names down the left side of VS Code.

The Hub walks through it in more detail: [Workspace Setup](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/workspace-setup.html)

## Now Open the Setup File

- **It is already in your workspace**, in the top folder: `00-check-your-setup.qmd`. Click it
- If you have no workspace yet, download the file on its own from the [Resources page](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/index.html), or click it here:
  [aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/00-check-your-setup.qmd](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/00-check-your-setup.qmd)
- It walks you through the rest, one gray box at a time, and it tells you what each box should print
- Work through it, and ask the moment something looks wrong, not at the end

## What "Working" Looks Like

The file finishes by running a checker we wrote for this course:

```r
library(v2v)
setup()
```

- You want a list of green check marks under **Required R packages**
- Red marks next to Quarto or Git are expected tonight if you have not finished those steps
- Red under Required is the one that needs me
- Then open the Command Palette and run **Check my setup**. It runs the same checklist and installs any package that is missing

## When It Breaks

- **Red text in R is not automatically an error.** R prints ordinary progress in red, so read the last line, not the color
- Close VS Code completely and reopen it. This genuinely fixes a lot
- If R asks "which would you like to update," choose **3: None**. The install command on the Hub already skips that prompt
- Run **Check my setup** from the Command Palette. It installs any missing package without the update question

## When It Still Breaks

- Send me the exact wording of the error, not a paraphrase. The wording is the diagnosis
- Ask after fifteen minutes stuck, not after two hours
- **Still stuck?** On github.com open your workspace repository, click **Code**, **Codespaces**, then **Create codespace on main**. R, the packages, and the Companion are already installed there

## Discussion: Good Enough Practices {.discuss}

On Wilson et al. (2017), "Good enough practices in scientific computing," answer each in
writing:

- The title concedes something. State what work "good enough" is doing in it, and who it is for
- Name one of their practices that would survive contact with your actual working habits, and one you would quietly abandon by October
- They write for the researcher with no formal computing training. State whether that framing makes the advice more usable or lowers the ceiling, and why
- Name one practice in the paper you think is oversold

## First Contact With the Data

[stream_log, November 2018]{.eyebrow}

| channel | game | viewers | date |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| sodapoppin | Marble It Up! | 27,934 | 1542578200214 |
| xqcow | Just Chatting | 19,381 | 1542578200240 |
| forsen | Artifact | 15,300 | 1542578200273 |
| giantwaffle | Rocket League | 4,697 | 1542578200423 |
| sodapoppin | Marble It Up! | 28,076 | 1542578261145 |
| xqcow | Just Chatting | 19,231 | 1542578261186 |

Look at the rows before reading on.

## The Data Moves

- This is a **time series**, not a snapshot: four channels recur across these rows
- Sodapoppin climbs from 27,934 to 28,076 to 28,203
- That is **269 viewers in 122 seconds**, an audience growing close to real time
- xQc lost 150 between the first two snapshots and then held, and Forsen lost 120
- Each number is a real moment: a clip went viral, a raid arrived, or bandwidth dropped

## The Timestamps Are Not Dates

- The date column is a thirteen-digit integer: 1542578200214
- The next row, 26 milliseconds later, reads 1542578200240
- That is **Unix epoch time**: milliseconds since midnight on January 1, 1970
- The gap between sodapoppin's first two rows is 60,931 milliseconds, about a minute
- Converting it is a wrangling step, not a research question, and Chapter 11 handles it

## Titles Are Themselves Data

- xQc's title is "RANK 1 GAMER ~ NO PLAN (help me)," which is a joke
- Forsen's title says he is giving away keys for a card game called Artifact
- Giantwaffle's title performs etiquette: "No Smoking in Chat"
- One title carries a literal line break, because the streamer's software let it through
- These are content analysis opportunities sitting in a column you might dismiss as metadata

## What the Package Gives You

- `twitch_chat_sample` holds roughly **35,000** chat messages from a 50-channel corpus
- `twitch_streams_sample` holds the stream snapshots for those channels, about **32,000** rows
- Helper functions wrap loading, codebook skeletons, reliability metrics, and diagnostics
- The helpers are not magic. They keep the concept from being buried under setup code
- `setup()` re-runs any time you suspect an installation problem

## Lock the Versions

- `renv.lock` is a file recording the exact version of every package your analysis used
- Without it, someone re-running your work next year may get different numbers, because a package changed underneath them

```r
renv::init()
```

- Run it before your first line of analysis code, and commit it before you collect your first data point

> "Back up (almost) everything created by a human being as soon as it is created. This includes scripts and programs of all kinds, software packages that your project depends on, and documentation."
>
> Wilson et al. (2017, p. 12)
